newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Maverick Nigerian rock star was bane of rulers.
newsitem.headline: Maverick Nigerian rock star was bane of rulers.

text.p: African rock legend Fela Anikulapo-Kuti, who died on Saturday, was long a thorn in the side of military governments in Nigeria, mixing his music with social criticism and advocacy of radical pan-Africanist ideas.
His "Afro-beat" music reached its peak in the 1970s when his outspoken social comment was expressed in songs that preached human dignity in Africa and abused soldiers who seized power.
"He is the first person to make democracy and human rights serious issues in Nigeria," said Nigerian journalist Dulue Mbachu.
Pro-democracy groups now proliferate in Africa's most populous nation, ruled by the military for 27 of its 37 years of independence from Britain.

Fela, who married more than two dozen women at one go and slept with hundreds of others, had his most spectacular clash with authorities in 1977 when soldiers stormed his house in Lagos which he had declared "Kalakuta Republic".
His mother was badly injured in the raid and died six months later. This also marked the beginning of his decline and loss of a fortune he had made from a successful music career.

Fela spent 18 months in jail in 1985 on a controversial charge of smuggling foreign exchange. He was freed after it emerged that the judge who convicted him had been under pressure by the then-military government to do so.
He formed a political party in 1979 which was disqualified from elections at the time, but towards the end of his life he turned his back on politics.
"No! No! I don't have interest in politics again," he told the opposition Tempo newspaper in February.
Fela was born on October 15, 1938, and received formal musical training at music college in Britain.
He returned home in 1963 and formed the Koola Lobitos band, playing a fusion of jazz and 'hilife'.
Koola Lobitos metamorphosed into Nigeria '70, later Africa '70 and finally Egypt '80 and became his medium for preaching African emancipation and lampooning the army rulers.

Fela's first break in the music business came in 1969 when he visited the United States and met members of the radical Black Panthers, who helped him set up a band in Nigeria to promote the African rock music he called "afro-beat".
By 1972, he was on his way to stardom with records that pulled no punches in criticising military rule in Nigeria.
In 1976, he topped the charts with "Zombie", which attacked soldiers as no more than machines following orders.

Fela was charged with armed robbery in 1981, a capital offence, but was acquitted. He told reporters later he had seen "hell in a police cell" and could no longer play his favourite instrument, the saxophone, because of throat injuries.

Fela came from a prominent Yoruba family of activists in Western Nigeria. His younger brother Beko Ransome-Kuti, a pro-democracy campaigner, was jailed for 15 years in 1995 for alleged involvement in a plot to topple the military government.
In the last two years, Fela had kept to himself at his Lagos home and only occasionally performed at The Shrine, his own club where he held the famous rap sessions he called 'yabbis'.
Rumour that Fela was dying had been rife in the local press, which inferred from his free-wheeling lifestyle that he might have been suffering from AIDS.
He initially refused treatment, having shunned both Western and native Nigerian medicine on principle.
The maverick musician, who among many quirks was famous for dressing only in his underpants, made little secret of a fondness for marijuana.

Anti-narcotics agents arrested him earlier this year for possessing the drug, and tried to reform his character and wean him off his habit. But Fela proved incorrigible and they finally had to admit defeat.
"I have been smoking for 40 years. It helps my music. People know I smoke worldwide. It is not drugs, it is grass," Fela said.
